title: Applied Chemistry and Chemistry in Service to Mankind

21.2 Cement, paper and pulp; the six heavy-chemical processes
21.3 Uses of common non-metals, metals, inorganic and organic compounds
21.4 Polymers, dyes, drugs, pesticides and fertilizers; colloids, osmotic pressure and buffers; radioisotopes

html:
Applied chemistry asks what happens when a balanced equation has to survive a factory, a market and the environment. This 3-question chapter is a rapid tour with a common logic: raw materials are prepared, converted, separated, finished and checked; the best process is not merely the one with the prettiest equation but the one giving safe, pure product at a defensible cost in energy, materials and pollution. The same thinking explains familiar materials — cement, paper, plastics, dyes, medicines and fertilizers — and the quiet chemistry of colloids, osmosis and buffers in daily life.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • A chemical plant runs: raw-material preparation → reaction/conversion → separation and purification → finishing/formulation → packaging, with quality control, utilities, recycle and waste treatment wrapped around every stage.
  • Batch processing (charge–react–discharge–clean) is flexible and traceable, suited to small-volume/many-product work such as pharmaceuticals. Continuous processing is steady, automated and economical at huge volume (ammonia, sulfuric acid, cement), but capital-heavy and inflexible.
  • Profit and sustainability turn on feedstock/energy price, yield and selectivity, catalyst life, recycle of unconverted reactants, co-product value, location, maintenance and pollution control. Green chemistry prefers prevention, atom economy, catalysis, safer solvents and energy efficiency over end-of-pipe cleanup.
  • Cement: limestone + clay are calcined and clinkered near 1450 °C; alite (C₃S) gives early strength, belite (C₂S) later strength. A little gypsum in grinding retards setting. Calcination itself releases CO₂: 1000 kg CaCO₃ → 440 kg CO₂.
  • Paper: fibres are liberated by mechanical pulping (high yield, lignin remains, paper yellows) or kraft chemical pulping (NaOH + Na₂S; strong fibres; black liquor is burned to recover energy/chemicals), then washed, bleached, formed on a wire, pressed and dried.
  • Heavy chemicals in one line each: Haber NH₃ (Fe catalyst, recycle); Ostwald HNO₃ (Pt–Rh gauze oxidizes NH₃); Contact H₂SO₄ (V₂O₅; SO₃ absorbed into oleum); chlor-alkali NaOH/Cl₂/H₂ (diaphragm historically, membrane cells now preferred); Solvay Na₂CO₃ (precipitate NaHCO₃, calcine); urea from NH₃ + CO₂ through ammonium carbamate (46% N).
  • Addition polymers grow by chain addition with no small by-product (polythene, PVC, polystyrene, Teflon). Condensation polymers eliminate a small molecule (nylon-6,6, PET, Bakelite). Thermoplastics soften reversibly; cross-linked thermosets do not. Vulcanization cross-links rubber with sulfur.
  • A dye needs a chromophore (for example –N=N– in azo dyes) and usually an auxochrome (–OH, –NH₂, –SO₃H) for solubility/fibre binding. Drugs are classified by action (analgesic, antibiotic, antacid…); antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, and misuse selects resistance.
  • Fertilizer labels give N–P₂O₅–K₂O percentages: urea 46-0-0, DAP about 18-46-0, muriate of potash about 0-0-60. Persistent fat-soluble pesticides such as DDT biomagnify; integrated pest management reduces chemical load.
  • Colloids (roughly 1–1000 nm dispersed particles) show Tyndall scattering and Brownian motion: milk (emulsion), fog (aerosol), jelly (gel), blood (sol). Alum coagulates colloidal clay in water treatment.
  • Osmotic pressure follows \pi = iCRT. About 0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood; reverse osmosis applies pressure greater than π to desalinate water. The blood buffer is chiefly H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻, holding pH near 7.4.
  • Radioisotopes: Tc-99m and F-18 for diagnostic imaging; I-131 for thyroid therapy; Co-60 for radiotherapy/sterilization and industrial radiography; Am-241 in smoke detectors. Protection is time, distance and shielding (ALARA).

21.1 The chemical industry: stages of production, economics and plant management, batch and continuous processing, environmental effects and their control

From flask to flowsheet

A commercial process is usually drawn as a chain of unit operations and unit processes:

  1. Feed preparation — crushing, dissolving, filtering, drying, preheating and purifying raw materials so the reactor receives a predictable diet.
  2. Conversion — the chemical reaction(s), controlled for temperature, pressure, residence time and catalyst contact. Conversion per pass may deliberately be modest (Haber) if unreacted feed can be recycled cheaply.
  3. Separation and purification — distillation, absorption, extraction, crystallization, filtration and drying. In many plants this block costs more energy than the reactor.
  4. Finishing — blending, granulation/prilling, polymerization shaping, tableting or dilution to specification.
  5. Packaging, storage and dispatch, with batch/lot traceability.

Around the chain sit utilities (steam, cooling water, compressed air, refrigeration), analytical quality control, recycle loops, flare/relief systems and effluent treatment. Scale-up is not just a bigger flask: surface area per volume falls, hot spots grow, mixing and heat removal become limiting, so pilot-plant data and hazard studies (for example HAZOP) precede a full plant.

Batch versus continuous, and what the manager optimizes

Feature Batch Continuous
Operation Load, react, unload, clean; one lot at a time Feed and product flow steadily
Best for Low volume, many grades, strict lot identity (medicines, dyes, speciality chemicals) Very large tonnage of one specification (NH₃, H₂SO₄, cement, refining)
Strengths Flexible scheduling/equipment, easier containment of a bad lot Labour/energy efficiency, steady quality, heat integration, automation
Weaknesses Downtime, cleaning waste, batch-to-batch variation High capital cost, difficult start-up/shutdown, poor flexibility

Plant economics is applied stoichiometry with prices attached. Yield and selectivity decide how much feed becomes saleable product rather than by-product; catalyst life and energy integration decide operating cost; capital is repaid over years, so utilization matters. A valuable co-product can rescue a process (acetone in the cumene route to phenol, Ch. 18), while a waste with no outlet can kill it (CaCl₂ brine from Solvay plants). Site choice balances raw material, water/energy, labour, market transport and environmental capacity. Good plant management is therefore chemistry plus preventive maintenance, instrumentation, inventory control, safety culture and documented quality systems.

Environmental effects and control

Typical burdens are acid gases (SO₂/NOₓ), particulates, volatile organic compounds and greenhouse gases to air; oxygen-demanding, acidic, saline or metal-bearing effluent to water; and sludges/ash/spent catalyst as solids. Control follows a hierarchy:

  • Prevent/substitute: choose catalytic, atom-economical routes; replace mercury cells by membrane cells; design out persistent products.
  • Recover/recycle: recycle unconverted reactants and solvents, burn pulping black liquor for energy and chemical recovery, use waste heat.
  • Treat at the boundary: electrostatic precipitators/bag filters for dust, lime scrubbers for SO₂, selective catalytic reduction for NOₓ, neutralization and biological oxidation for effluent, secure disposal of hazardous residues.
  • Monitor and account: continuous emission monitoring, environmental impact assessment before construction, and increasingly carbon capture or low-carbon hydrogen for the hardest sectors (cement, ammonia, steel).
Worked example 21.1 — the CO₂ locked inside limestone

Problem. A cement kiln calcines 1000 kg of pure CaCO₃. What mass of process CO₂ is released before any fuel is counted? (CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹, CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹.)

Solution. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ is 1:1 in moles. Mass of CO₂ = 1000 × 44/100 = 440 kg. That is why cement decarbonization cannot be solved by clean fuel alone: nearly half a tonne of CO₂ per tonne of limestone is chemistry, so clinker substitution and carbon capture matter as much as kiln fuel.

Urea's nitrogen, by the label

Problem. Fertiliser sacks proclaim urea CO(NH₂)₂ as 46 % nitrogen. Verify the claim from the formula (C 12, O 16, N 14, H 1), and state why urea outranks ammonium sulphate as a nitrogen source. Solution. Molar mass = 12 + 16 + 2 × (14 + 2) = 60 g/mol; the two nitrogens weigh 28 g, so the mass fraction is 28/60 = 0.4667, i.e. 46.7 %, labelled 46 % — the richest solid nitrogen fertiliser in common use, against ammonium sulphate's 21 %, and it leaves no acid residue in the soil the way the sulphate does.

21.2 Cement, paper and pulp; the six heavy-chemical processes

Portland cement

The raw mix is mainly limestone (CaCO₃) with clay/shale supplying SiO₂, Al₂O₃ and Fe₂O₃, corrected with sand or iron ore where needed. In the modern dry process the ground, homogenized meal passes through preheaters, calcines near 900 °C and enters a rotary kiln at about 1450 °C, emerging as marble-sized clinker. Its strength minerals are alite (3CaO·SiO₂, “C₃S”, early strength), belite (2CaO·SiO₂, “C₂S”, later strength), tricalcium aluminate (C₃A, rapid early reaction/heat) and ferrite (C₄AF). The clinker is ground with about 3–5% gypsum, which retards the otherwise flash-setting hydration of C₃A.

Ordinary Portland cement (OPC) is essentially clinker + gypsum. Portland pozzolana cement (PPC) intergrinds reactive material such as fly ash; the pozzolan later consumes Ca(OH)₂ from hydration to make more binding calcium-silicate-hydrate, often improving durability and lowering clinker-related CO₂. Setting and hardening are hydration, not “drying”: silicates form C–S–H gel plus Ca(OH)₂ exothermically, which is why fresh concrete is cured wet and why the alkaline pore solution passivates reinforcing steel.

Pulp and paper

Paper is a felted web of cellulose fibres. The industrial problem is freeing those fibres from lignin, the aromatic glue of wood. Mechanical pulping grinds or refines wood with high yield, but lignin remains, so newsprint is weaker and yellows in light. Kraft (chemical) pulping cooks chips in NaOH + Na₂S (“white liquor”), dissolving lignin to give strong fibres; the spent black liquor is concentrated and burned, recovering both energy and inorganic cooking chemicals. Pulp is washed, screened and bleached — modern sequences use oxygen, chlorine dioxide (elemental-chlorine-free) or peroxide rather than elemental chlorine, reducing chlorinated pollutants.

Stock is then diluted, mixed with fillers (CaCO₃/kaolin for opacity and smoothness) and sizing agents (to resist ink spreading), spread on a moving wire (Fourdrinier machine), pressed, dried on heated cylinders and calendered. Paper quality is specified by grammage (g m⁻²), tensile/burst/tear strength, brightness, opacity and moisture. Recovered paper is repulped and de-inked, though fibres shorten a little each cycle. Bamboo, bagasse, straw and sabai grass are regionally important non-wood fibres, including in South Asian mills.

Six processes the syllabus names

Product Heart of the process Non-negotiable examination point
Ammonia — Haber N₂ + 3H₂ over promoted Fe, about 450 °C and 200 atm, NH₃ liquefied out and unreacted gas recycled Exothermic equilibrium compromise; catalyst changes rate, not equilibrium
Nitric acid — Ostwald 4NH₃ + 5O₂ →(Pt–Rh gauze, about 900 °C) 4NO + 6H₂O; 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 3NO₂ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ + NO (recycled) The NO by-product is not waste; it re-enters oxidation/absorption
Sulfuric acid — Contact S or sulfide ore → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅ near 450 °C; SO₃ absorbed in conc. H₂SO₄ to oleum, then diluted Directly dissolving SO₃ in water makes a corrosive acid mist
Caustic soda — chlor-alkali Electrolysis of brine: anode Cl₂, cathode H₂ + NaOH. A porous diaphragm limits Cl₂/OH⁻ mixing but gives salt-contaminated liquor Modern membrane cells give purer NaOH and avoid asbestos diaphragms/mercury cells
Sodium carbonate — Solvay NH₃/CO₂ into brine precipitates NaHCO₃; calcining gives Na₂CO₃; lime recovers NH₃ Overall waste stream is mainly CaCl₂; KHCO₃ is too soluble for a potassium version (Ch. 14)
Urea 2NH₃ + CO₂ under pressure → ammonium carbamate → CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O; solution is concentrated and prilled/granulated 46% N — the most concentrated common solid nitrogen fertilizer; excess heat forms undesirable biuret
Worked example — why industry picks a compromise temperature (Haber process)

Ammonia synthesis, N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, is exothermic. Reason through the plant conditions as an examiner does:

  1. Yield at equilibrium (Le Chatelier): low temperature and high pressure favour NH₃ (4 gas moles → 2).
  2. Rate: low temperature is uselessly slow; a catalyst (finely divided iron) speeds the approach to equilibrium but cannot change its position.
  3. Economics: very high pressures need expensive plant.

So the operating point is a compromise: about 450 °C, about 200 atm, iron catalyst, with the ammonia liquefied out and unreacted gases recycled. The same three-line argument (yield ↔ rate ↔ cost) answers the equivalent Contact-process question (about 450 °C, 1–2 atm, V₂O₅ catalyst).

Trap — batch vs continuous, and what a catalyst cannot do

Continuous processes suit bulk chemicals made on a huge scale (ammonia, sulphuric acid, cement); batch processing suits small-scale, high-value products (many drugs and dyes). And the perennial trap: a catalyst lowers activation energy and shortens the time to equilibrium — it never increases the percentage yield at equilibrium.

21.4 Polymers, dyes, drugs, pesticides and fertilizers; colloids, osmotic pressure and buffers; radioisotopes

Polymers

A polymer is a macromolecule built from repeating monomer units. Addition polymers form when π bonds open in a chain reaction and no small molecule is lost: ethene → polythene, chloroethene → PVC, styrene → polystyrene, tetrafluoroethene → PTFE (Teflon). Condensation polymers grow stepwise with loss of H₂O or another small molecule: hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid → nylon-6,6; ethylene glycol + terephthalic acid → PET polyester; phenol + formaldehyde → Bakelite. Natural rubber is cis-polyisoprene; heating it with sulfur (vulcanization) introduces cross-links that convert a sticky gum into a resilient elastomer. Linear/branched thermoplastics soften on heating and can be remoulded; cross-linked thermosets char rather than melt. Fibres (nylon, polyester) are drawn into oriented chains for tensile strength. The current materials challenge is circular: design for sorting/recycling, reduce microplastic shedding and reserve biodegradable polymers such as PLA for settings where their required composting conditions actually exist.

Dyes

Colour requires conjugated unsaturation. The group chiefly responsible is the chromophore — azo –N=N–, carbonyl/anthraquinone systems, phthalocyanine rings — while an auxochrome such as –NH₂, –OH or –SO₃H deepens colour and helps the dye dissolve or bind. Azo dyes are made by diazotizing a primary aromatic amine and coupling it with phenol/ β-naphthol (Ch. 20). By application, dyes may be direct (hydrogen-bond to cotton), acid (anionic, for wool/nylon), basic (cationic), reactive (covalent bond to fibre — excellent wash fastness), vat (indigo; applied in reduced soluble form, then oxidized in the fibre) or disperse (tiny particles for polyester). Some azo dyes can be metabolically cleaved to regulated aromatic amines, so dye chemistry is also toxicology.

Drugs

A drug is a substance used to diagnose, prevent or treat disease. Examples by action: analgesics/antipyretics (paracetamol; aspirin is also anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet), antibiotics (penicillins and others act on bacterial targets and are useless against viral colds; incomplete or unnecessary courses select resistant bacteria), antacids (Mg(OH)₂/Al(OH)₃ mixtures neutralize excess gastric HCl), antihistamines (allergy), antimalarials (chloroquine historically, artemisinin combinations now central), and anaesthetics. An antiseptic is applied to living tissue (chloroxylenol/Dettol-type preparations, iodine tincture); a disinfectant is for surfaces (phenolics, hypochlorite) and is generally more cytotoxic. Dose, formulation and pharmacokinetics turn a molecule into a medicine — the bridge to pharmacology in the health-science degrees CEE opens.

Pesticides and fertilizers

Pesticides are named by target: insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, rodenticides. Organochlorines such as DDT are persistent and fat-soluble, so they biomagnify through food chains and are heavily restricted. Organophosphates/carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase and can be acutely poisonous to handlers. Pyrethroids mimic natural pyrethrins; biopesticides include Bacillus thuringiensis preparations and neem (azadirachtin). Copper-based Bordeaux mixture remains a classic fungicide. Integrated pest management — resistant varieties, crop rotation, biological control, monitoring and targeted spraying — keeps chemical use as the last, measured resort.

Plants need N for protein/chlorophyll, P for ATP/nucleic acids/roots and K for enzyme and water regulation. Fertilizer grades quote N–P₂O₅–K₂O: urea 46-0-0, ammonium sulfate 21-0-0 (plus sulfur), single/triple superphosphate about 16/46% P₂O₅, DAP about 18-46-0 and muriate of potash (KCl) about 0-0-60. In soil, urease hydrolyses urea to ammonium, nitrifying bacteria form nitrate, and excess nitrate/phosphate leaches or runs off to cause eutrophication. Manures and composts are dilute and slow but add carbon and improve soil structure; the modern answer is soil testing and the right dose at the right time, not “chemical versus organic” slogans.

Colloids, osmosis and buffers around us

A colloid disperses particles of roughly 1–1000 nm through a continuous medium. Named by the pair of phases, examples include sols (paint, blood plasma proteins), gels (jelly, silica gel), emulsions (milk, mayonnaise: liquid in liquid), foams (whipped cream, shaving foam) and aerosols (fog, smoke). Colloids scatter a light beam (Tyndall effect), jitter under molecular bombardment (Brownian motion) and often carry surface charge, so electrolytes coagulate them — multivalent ions being most effective (Hardy–Schulze pattern). Alum clarifies turbid water by coagulating negatively charged clay and humic colloids; gelatin and casein act as protective colloids in foods and inks.

Osmosis is net solvent movement through a semipermeable membrane toward the side of higher solute concentration; osmotic pressure is \pi=iCRT. A 0.9% (9 g L⁻¹) NaCl solution is about 0.154 mol L⁻¹ in NaCl and, with i≈2, close to blood osmolality — hence “normal saline” neither swells nor shrivels red cells. Salt and sugar preserve food by drawing water from microbes; wilted vegetables crisp again in water; and reverse osmosis applies pressure exceeding π to force fresh water out of seawater/brackish supplies. Oral rehydration (also Ch. 15) is osmosis harnessed by coupled Na⁺–glucose absorption.

A buffer is a conjugate acid–base pair that absorbs added H⁺ or OH⁻ with little pH change. Blood is held near pH 7.4 chiefly by H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻, assisted by phosphate and proteins including haemoglobin; acetate and phosphate buffers stabilize laboratory reagents, eye drops, injections and fermentation media. The chemistry is Ch. 7's equilibrium doing daily work.

Medical and industrial uses of radioisotopes

Unstable nuclei are useful because their radiation can be detected at tracer mass or focused for damage. Tc-99m (metastable, 6 h half-life, clean γ) is the workhorse of diagnostic scans of bone, heart and thyroid; F-18 in fluorodeoxyglucose lights up glucose-hungry tissue in PET imaging. I-131 is concentrated by the thyroid, where its β emission treats hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer; P-32 has been used for excess red-cell production; Co-60 γ beams treat tumours and sterilize medical supplies; Ir-192 seeds deliver brachytherapy; and targeted agents such as Lu-177 combine a tumour-seeking molecule with a β emitter (“theranostics” when paired with an imaging isotope).

Industry uses Co-60/Ir-192 γ radiography to inspect welds and castings, β/γ gauges to measure sheet thickness and tank levels without contact, tracer isotopes to find pipeline leaks and follow groundwater, Am-241 ionization in smoke detectors, food irradiation to delay sprouting and kill insects/microbes, and sterile-insect releases against pests. In research, ³H, ¹⁴C, ³²P and ³⁵S labels trace metabolic pathways, while ¹⁴C dating reads archaeological time (Ch. 12). Every benefit is paired with ALARA discipline — minimize time, maximize distance, use appropriate shielding, and manage decaying waste by half-life.

Common mistake

Five distinctions the paper probes: the catalyst speeds the Haber reaction while the promoters keep the iron porous and active — not the same job; oleum is SO₃ dissolved in sulphuric acid, not in water, because water makes an acid mist; the diaphragm separates products, not electrodes from solution — without it Cl₂ and NaOH marry into hypochlorite; gypsum retards cement's setting rather than strengthening it; and isotonic saline matches blood's osmotic pressure at 0.9 %, while distilled water in a vein would burst the cells.

Chapter summary

  • A viable process joins reaction chemistry to separation, recycle, energy, quality and waste systems; batch suits variety, continuous suits volume.
  • Cement clinker minerals and gypsum explain strength and setting, while limestone calcination makes process CO₂ unavoidable without substitution/capture.
  • Kraft pulping's chemical-recovery loop is why a paper mill can be both a fibre factory and a power station.
  • Haber, Ostwald, Contact, chlor-alkali, Solvay and urea each compress to one catalyst/reagent, one equilibrium trick and one product-separation trick.
  • Uses of common substances are predictable from properties such as conductivity, oxide passivation, alkalinity, π reactivity and hydrogen bonding.
  • Addition versus condensation polymerization, chromophore/auxochrome design and drug action classes organize the consumer-chemical world.
  • Fertilizer value is printed as N–P₂O₅–K₂O; pesticide persistence and nutrient runoff are the environmental price of careless dosage.
  • Tyndall scattering identifies colloids, iCRT prices osmosis from saline drips to desalination, and bicarbonate keeps blood near pH 7.4.
  • Radioisotopes image, treat, sterilize, inspect and trace — always under time–distance–shielding discipline.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — reactors rarely give a pure, saleable stream; separation is the next core block.

2. (a) — steady operation amortizes automation and heat-integration over huge throughput.

3. (c) — yield = conversion × selectivity in process language.

4. (b) — wet limestone/lime scrubbing converts SO₂ to sulfite/sulfate (gypsum) salts.

5. (a) — clay supplies silica, alumina and iron oxide.

6. (d) — sulfate controls C₃A hydration and prevents flash set.

7. (b) — partial melting at clinkering temperature forms alite.

8. (c) — sulfide improves lignin cleavage and pulp strength in kraft cooking.
